summary: Typhon (also called Typhoeus, Typhaon, or Typhos) was a monstrous serpentine giant and one of the deadliest creatures in Greek mythology. According to Hesiod he was the youngest child of Gaia (Earth) and Tartarus, though other sources make him the son of Hera alone or of Cronus. He challenged Zeus for supremacy over the cosmos in a cataclysmic battle, but was defeated by the god's thunderbolts and imprisoned beneath Mount Etna (or the island of Ischia), where his fury was held responsible for volcanic activity. By his mate Echidna he fathered many of the most famous monsters of myth, including Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera, and the Sphinx.
etymology: Several derivations of the name have been proposed. Some connect it to the Greek words for "whirlwind" (tuphon, tuphos), fitting Typhon's role as father of the destructive storm-winds, while others derive it from a root meaning "smoke," linking it to his volcanic associations. Another proposal traces it to an Indo-European root meaning "abyss," making him a "Serpent of the Deep," and some scholars suggest a Phoenician origin connected with Mount Kasios (Jebel Aqra). His name is also thought to have influenced the Persian tūfān, an ancestor of the meteorological term "typhoon."

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: Birth: In Hesiod's account Typhon is the offspring of Gaia (Earth) and Tartarus, produced after Zeus had defeated the Titans. Alternative traditions make him the child of Hera alone (as in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo) or of Cronus. Several sources locate his birthplace in Cilicia, particularly near the Corycian cave and the coastal city of Corycus (modern Kızkalesi, Turkey).

Descriptions: Typhon possessed extraordinary and terrifying features. Hesiod gives him a hundred snake heads with dark, flickering tongues, from which fire and dreadful sounds issued. He was depicted as a winged humanoid with serpent tails for legs. Later writers expand the picture: Apollodorus describes him as so vast that his head often brushed the stars, and Nonnus provides the most elaborate version, giving him many animal heads (leopards, lions, bulls, boars, bears, wolves, dogs), two hundred hands, and the ability to spit poison.

Offspring: By his mate Echidna, Typhon fathered a brood of legendary monsters, among them Orthrus the two-headed dog, Cerberus the multi-headed guardian of Hades, the regenerating Lernaean Hydra, the fire-breathing Chimera, the Caucasian Eagle that tormented Prometheus, Ladon the dragon of the Hesperides, the Sphinx, and the Nemean Lion. Still later sources add the Colchian dragon, Scylla, and the Gorgon.

sections.heading: Battle with Zeus
paragraphs: In Hesiod's version the contest is a straightforward divine victory: Zeus employs his thunderbolts to overcome Typhon swiftly, hurling him down as "a maimed wreck." The struggle is presented as the final challenge to Zeus's newly won cosmic order.

Apollodorus gives a much-extended account. The gods, terrified, transform into animals and flee to Egypt; Typhon at first overpowers Zeus and severs his sinews, which Hermes and Aegipan recover from the Corycian cave. The Moirai (Fates) then weaken Typhon with "ephemeral fruits," and he is finally defeated in Sicily when Zeus casts Mount Etna upon him.

Nonnus's Dionysiaca (late 4th or early 5th century AD) offers the most elaborate retelling. Typhon steals Zeus's thunderbolts, but Cadmus enchants him with panpipes to recover the weapons. After a sustained and devastating battle that wreaks havoc on the natural world, Typhon is at last defeated and buried beneath Sicily.

sections.heading: Burial and volcanic activity
paragraphs: The most common tradition places Typhon imprisoned beneath Mount Etna in Sicily, with the volcano's eruptions attributed to his rage; Pindar describes him lying in "dread Tartarus" yet also pinned under Etna. An alternative locates him beneath the island of Ischia in the Phlegraean Islands off Naples, and some accounts stretch his prison across the volcanic regions from Sicily to Cumae, including Mount Vesuvius.

Other burial sites are also recorded. A mountain near Thebes in Boeotia called Typhaonium suggests an early local tradition, while some sources place Typhon beneath Lake Serbonis (modern Lake Bardawil) in Egypt.

Homer refers to a place called the "couch of Typhoeus" in the land of the Arimoi, whose location both ancient and modern scholars dispute. Proposed identifications include Cilicia (near the Calycadnus river and the Corycian cave), Mount Kasios (Jebel Aqra) in Syria, Catacecaumene in Lydia, and Ischia; Strabo connected Ischia's Greek name Pithecussae ("monkeys") with an Etruscan word for monkeys, arimoi.

sections.heading: Comparative mythology
paragraphs: Succession myth: The Typhonomachy forms the climax of Hesiod's larger succession narrative — Uranus overthrown by Cronus, Cronus by Zeus, and finally Zeus challenged by Typhon. Zeus's ultimate victory confirms him as the supreme cosmic ruler.

Python and Delphyne: Typhon is closely associated with other monstrous offspring of Gaia. Python, the guardian serpent of Delphi slain by Apollo, shares similar parentage and the motif of an Olympian killing a great serpent in single combat. Delphyne, the she-dragon who served as Typhon's foster-mother, like Echidna was half-maid and half-snake, and both serpents are connected with Corycian caves.

Near Eastern influence: Scholars widely accept that the Typhon myth was shaped by ancient Near Eastern antecedents. Mesopotamian parallels include Ninurta's battles with Asag and with the winged Anzû, and Marduk's defeat of Tiamat to win kingship. Myths of the Mount Kasios region — Baal Sapon against Yamm in Ugaritic tradition, Tarhunna against Illuyanka among the Hittites, and Teshub against Hedammu and Ullikummi — are viewed as origins of the Zeus–Typhon battle. From about 500 BC, the Greeks identified Typhon with the Egyptian chaos-god Set, defeated by Horus (equated with Apollo) and hidden in the Serbonian marsh.

sections.heading: Confusion with the Giants
paragraphs: Typhon closely resembles the Giants, the older offspring of Gaia who likewise challenged Zeus, were depicted as snake-footed, and were said to be buried under volcanoes. In early sources the two are kept distinct, but later writers — including the author of the Fabulae, Horace, and Nonnus — counted Typhon among the Giants.

In this later conflation Typhon is sometimes shown fighting Athena alongside the Giants Mimas, Porphyrion, and Enceladus during the Gigantomachy, blurring the line between his solitary rebellion and the collective revolt of the Giants.
